text: What is an exoplanet?
choices: A planet orbiting a star beyond the Sun
A moon orbiting a planet
A star without a companion
A comet entering a planetary system

text: What does a transit method detect when an exoplanet crosses its star?
choices: A permanent increase in the star's mass
A temporary dip in the star's brightness
A burst of radio waves from the planet
A change in the star's color caused by fusion

text: What stellar motion is measured by the radial-velocity method?
choices: Motion only across the sky
Rotation around the star's poles
Motion toward and away from the observer
Motion of the planet's atmosphere

text: Why does a transiting planet make its star appear slightly fainter?
choices: The planet turns off part of the star's fusion
The planet absorbs all of the star's heat
The planet pulls the star farther from Earth
The planet blocks part of the star's light

text: Which object is normally the light source monitored during an exoplanet transit survey?
choices: The host star
The planet's moon
A distant galaxy
An asteroid belt

text: What makes repeated, evenly spaced transits especially useful?
choices: They prove the planet has an atmosphere
They reveal a likely orbital period
They measure the planet's magnetic field directly
They show that the star is not rotating

text: In a transit light curve, what does the depth of the dip mainly indicate?
choices: The planet's surface temperature
The star's distance from the galaxy center
The planet-to-star radius ratio
The planet's atmospheric pressure

text: What causes the Doppler shift used in radial-velocity measurements?
choices: A planet changes the chemical elements in its star
Dust removes only blue photons
A telescope magnifies the star's spectrum
Relative motion changes the observed wavelengths of stellar lines

text: Which NASA mission famously used a large field of view to search for transiting exoplanets?
choices: Kepler
Cassini
Juno
New Horizons

text: What is TESS primarily designed to find?
choices: Comets entering the Oort Cloud
Transiting planets around relatively bright nearby stars
Gravitational waves from merging black holes
Volcanoes on Jupiter's moons

text: What is the habitable zone around a star?
choices: The region containing every planet with life
The area where stars cannot produce flares
The orbital region where surface liquid water could be possible
The ring where all planets have Earth-like gravity

text: What is a hot Jupiter?
choices: A rocky planet with active volcanoes
A Jupiter-sized moon heated by tides
A planet that orbits only red giant stars
A large gas giant in a very close, short-period orbit

text: Why are close-in giant planets often easier to detect with radial velocity?
choices: Their short orbits and large masses produce a larger, faster stellar wobble
They emit more visible light than their stars
They always pass directly between Earth and the star
Their atmospheres amplify the star's spectral lines

text: What does direct imaging attempt to record?
choices: Only the star's radial velocity
Light from the planet separated from its host star's glare
A planet's interior seismic waves
The shadow of a planet on a distant galaxy

text: What physical effect makes gravitational microlensing sensitive to planets?
choices: A planet reflects a laser beam toward Earth
A star's atmosphere refracts the planet's radio signal
A foreground system bends and magnifies light from a background star
A planet periodically blocks a background galaxy

text: What does astrometry measure in an exoplanet search?
choices: The brightness of a planet's aurora
The depth of a planet's ocean
The temperature of a starspot
A star's tiny position wobble on the sky

text: If an exoplanet has a longer orbital period, what generally happens to the spacing between its transits?
choices: The transits are farther apart
The transits become permanently deeper
The star stops showing spectral lines
The planet loses its orbital inclination

text: What is the semi-major axis of an orbit?
choices: The altitude of the planet's atmosphere
Half the length of the orbit's longest diameter
The radius of the host star
The angle between the orbit and the sky

text: Which orbital orientation gives the highest chance of seeing a transit?
choices: An orbit viewed face-on
An orbit perpendicular to the planet's motion
An orbit nearly edge-on to the observer
An orbit with zero stellar mass

text: Why can an eclipsing binary mimic a planetary transit?
choices: Its planets always have the same radius as stars
Binary stars cannot be resolved by any telescope
The binary's radio emission blocks visible light
A faint binary companion can produce a periodic brightness dip

text: What observation helps confirm that a transit signal is caused by a planet rather than an instrumental artifact?
choices: Independent observations showing the same periodic signal
A single unusually deep data point
A spectrum with no stellar lines
A larger telescope mirror pointed elsewhere

text: What can transmission spectroscopy reveal about an exoplanet?
choices: The exact number of rocks on its surface
Wavelength-dependent absorption by gases in its atmosphere
Its core's crystal structure directly
Its host star's age without any model

text: Why is infrared observing valuable for many exoplanet atmospheres?
choices: Infrared telescopes do not need to block starlight
Infrared light travels faster than visible light
Many molecules have strong vibrational features in infrared wavelengths
Planets emit no infrared radiation of their own

text: What does an exoplanet's secondary eclipse measure?
choices: The first time the planet crosses in front of its star
The planet's orbital tilt from astrometry alone
The star's birth in a molecular cloud
The system's light when the planet passes behind its star

text: What is a super-Earth?
choices: A planet more massive than Earth but less massive than the ice giants
A planet with a surface proven to be superhabitable
A moon larger than Jupiter
Any planet orbiting a star larger than the Sun

text: What is a sub-Neptune, in common exoplanet usage?
choices: A planet orbiting below Neptune's orbit in our solar system
A planet smaller than Neptune, often with a substantial volatile envelope
A moon inside Neptune's atmosphere
A star whose temperature is below Neptune's

text: What is a planet's orbital eccentricity?
choices: Its atmospheric concentration of carbon
Its distance from the center of its galaxy
A number describing how much its orbit departs from a circle
The fraction of its surface covered by ocean

text: What is a planet's albedo?
choices: The speed at which it rotates
The mass of its atmosphere
The length of its year
The fraction of incoming light it reflects

text: What does equilibrium temperature estimate?
choices: A planet's idealized temperature from absorbed and emitted radiation
The temperature measured at the planet's core
The exact daily surface weather
The temperature at which its star begins fusion

text: Why might a planet orbiting a red dwarf be tidally locked?
choices: Red dwarfs emit no gravity
Tidal forces can synchronize its rotation with its short orbital period
Its atmosphere forces it to stop rotating
The planet is always captured by a passing comet

text: What is tidal locking?
choices: A process that removes a planet from its star
A method for locking a telescope onto a target
A state in which one rotation takes the same time as one orbit
A resonance between two unrelated galaxies

text: What is an exomoon?
choices: A small star orbiting a planet
A moon located beyond our solar system but not orbiting anything
An artificial satellite around Earth's Moon
A natural satellite orbiting an exoplanet

text: What is a rogue planet?
choices: A planet not gravitationally bound to a star
A planet with an unusually large moon
A planet whose orbit is exactly circular
A planet that has been directly visited by a probe

text: Which star hosted the first exoplanet found orbiting a Sun-like star?
choices: Sirius
51 Pegasi
Betelgeuse
Vega

text: What is notable about Proxima Centauri b?
choices: It is the largest exoplanet ever measured
It was discovered by imaging its oceans
It is a nearby planet orbiting the red dwarf Proxima Centauri
It orbits the star Polaris

text: What is distinctive about the TRAPPIST-1 system?
choices: It contains seven stars all orbiting one planet
It is the only system with a hot Jupiter
It was discovered by a lunar lander
It contains seven known Earth-sized planets around a very small star

text: Why is Kepler-186f historically interesting?
choices: It was an early Earth-size planet found in a star's habitable zone
It is the first planet ever detected by any method
It is a directly imaged gas giant with rings
It orbits a neutron star at the speed of light

text: What was unusual about HD 209458 b's early characterization?
choices: It was the first planet found around a pulsar
It was among the first transiting planets whose atmosphere was studied
It has no host star
It was detected only through a galaxy's rotation

text: What does a transit's duration depend on besides the orbital period?
choices: Only the planet's atmospheric color
Only the number of moons
The star's size, the orbit's geometry, and the planet's speed
The host galaxy's total mass

text: What does a radial-velocity semi-amplitude describe?
choices: The planet's diameter measured during transit
The amount of reflected light from the planet
The width of the star's habitable zone
The size of the star's line-of-sight velocity variation

text: Why are multiple transits needed to establish an orbital period confidently?
choices: A period requires measuring the interval between repeated events
One transit always measures the planet's mass exactly
The first transit cannot be seen in visible light
A second transit removes the star's atmosphere

text: What is the main role of adaptive optics in direct imaging?
choices: It increases a planet's intrinsic brightness
It corrects atmospheric blurring to improve angular resolution
It changes infrared photons into radio waves
It measures the planet's mass through chemistry

text: What does a coronagraph do in exoplanet imaging?
choices: It enlarges the planet's atmosphere
It creates a transit in the light curve
It suppresses light from the host star
It removes a planet's reflected light

text: What is transit timing variation (TTV)?
choices: A change in transit color caused by clouds
A timing error caused only by Earth's rotation
The interval between a star's flares
A change in the expected time of a planet's transit caused by gravitational interactions

text: Why is being in the habitable zone not proof that a planet is habitable?
choices: Atmosphere, climate, and geological conditions also determine surface habitability
Every habitable-zone planet is hidden by its star
The habitable zone exists only around binary stars
Liquid water is impossible outside Earth's orbit

text: What is the Rossiter–McLaughlin effect used to investigate?
choices: The abundance of water in a planet's core
The alignment between a planet's orbit and its star's rotation
The planet's gravitational lensing mass
The number of stars in the host cluster

text: What does stellar metallicity mean in exoplanet studies?
choices: The fraction of a star made only of iron
The star's surface reflectivity
The abundance of elements heavier than helium in a star
The number of planets made of metal

text: Why can planets around active stars be harder to characterize?
choices: Active stars have no measurable spectra
Activity removes the planet's gravitational pull
Active stars cannot host planets
Starspots and flares can imitate or obscure planetary signals

text: What is the primary advantage of combining transit and radial-velocity data?
choices: Together they can yield both planetary radius and mass
Together they prove a planet has life
They eliminate the need to observe the host star
They directly photograph the planet's surface

text: Why is the mass of a transiting planet useful with its radius?
choices: It determines the planet's exact cloud map
The pair gives its bulk density and constrains composition
It identifies every moon automatically
It measures the host star's age without uncertainty

text: What is radial-velocity stellar jitter?
choices: A planet's rapid change in atmospheric pressure
A telescope's deliberate movement between targets
Apparent velocity variation produced by stellar activity rather than an orbiting planet
The velocity of a star leaving its galaxy

text: Why can a starspot crossing during a transit matter?
choices: It proves the planet has a magnetic field
It removes limb darkening from the data
It directly measures the planet's ocean salinity
It can reveal stellar surface structure and bias the inferred transit depth

text: What is limb darkening in a stellar transit light curve?
choices: The stellar disk appears dimmer toward its edge than at its center
The planet darkens its own limb during an eclipse
A star's outer layers become transparent at night
The host star's poles stop rotating

text: What is the impact parameter of a transit?
choices: The impact speed of a planet striking its star
The projected distance of the transit chord from the star's center, scaled by stellar radius
The planet's mass divided by its orbital period
The angular distance between two host stars

text: Why does a grazing transit make the planet's radius harder to infer?
choices: It makes the host star emit no photons
It guarantees that the planet has rings
The shallow chord and geometry create stronger radius–impact-parameter degeneracies
It changes the planet's mass into a lower value

text: What is photometric dilution in transit analysis?
choices: The planet scatters all photons out of the aperture
Stellar activity increases the true transit depth
A detector converts every transit into a radial-velocity signal
Unrelated or companion-star light makes the observed transit shallower

text: What key quantity is left ambiguous by a single-lined radial-velocity orbit?
choices: The true planet mass, because the measurement gives M sin(i)
The star's spectral type, because no lines are present
The orbital period, because velocities have no time information
The planet's radius, because velocity measures a shadow

text: What does the argument of periastron specify?
choices: The tilt of a star's magnetic field
The orientation of an eccentric orbit's closest-approach point
The radius of the planet's atmosphere
The direction of a telescope's primary mirror

text: What does a secondary-eclipse depth most directly constrain for a hot planet?
choices: Its nightside ocean depth
Its exact bulk mass
Its dayside emitted and reflected flux relative to the star
The host star's parallax

text: What is a phase curve in exoplanet photometry?
choices: A plot of stellar mass against metallicity
A map of detector pixels during a transit
A curve showing only a planet's formation age
Brightness variation over an orbit as the visible illuminated fraction and thermal emission change

text: Why does an atmospheric transmission spectrum often contain only a few scale heights of signal?
choices: The atmosphere changes the planet's effective radius by only a small amount relative to the star
The atmosphere blocks the star completely at every wavelength
A spectrum measures only the planet's solid core
Telescope mirrors remove all spectral structure

text: Why can high-altitude clouds flatten a transmission spectrum?
choices: They increase the star's radius during transit
They set an opaque altitude that hides deeper molecular absorption layers
They turn all atmospheric molecules into oxygen
They cause the planet to stop transiting

text: What is a common degeneracy in interpreting a nearly featureless transmission spectrum?
choices: Only nitrogen and only oxygen always have identical spectra
A spectrum cannot depend on temperature
High clouds, hazes, low abundances, and a high mean molecular weight can produce similar spectra
A flat spectrum uniquely proves an airless planet

text: Why is atmospheric retrieval not simply a direct lookup of molecular abundances?
choices: Molecules emit no wavelength-dependent features
Retrievals use only the planet's orbital period
Every exoplanet has the same pressure profile
Different atmospheric structures and assumptions can reproduce the same noisy spectrum

text: What does a retrieval prior do in Bayesian exoplanet spectroscopy?
choices: It represents assumptions about plausible parameter values before the data are applied
It removes the need for a likelihood function
It converts a transit into an image
It guarantees the most abundant molecule is detected

text: What is the photoevaporation radius valley?
choices: A gap between a star's photosphere and chromosphere
A deficit of close-in planets between roughly super-Earth and sub-Neptune sizes
A missing region in direct images caused by a coronagraph
A lack of planets beyond the snow line

text: How does core-powered mass loss differ from photoevaporation?
choices: It applies only to planets with metallic cores
It describes mass transfer between two stars
It uses a planet's own cooling luminosity to help remove its atmosphere rather than primarily stellar high-energy heating
It requires a planet to be outside every habitable zone

text: What climate outcome is associated with a runaway greenhouse?
choices: A planet freezes because all water condenses permanently
A star's core collapses into a planet
The atmosphere becomes pure molecular hydrogen
Increasing water vapor drives strong warming that can prevent a stable surface ocean

text: Why are flares a special concern for planets around many M dwarfs?
choices: Frequent ultraviolet and X-ray outbursts can erode atmospheres and alter photochemistry
Flares remove the star's gravitational field for hours
M dwarfs never have habitable zones
Flares make radial velocity physically impossible

text: What is finite-source magnification in a microlensing event?
choices: The lens star's radius is set to zero in the model
The source star's nonzero angular size smooths and limits the ideal point-source magnification
A planet's atmosphere magnifies its own reflected light
A detector averages all stars in the galaxy

text: Why is direct imaging favored for young giant planets?
choices: Their transits are always deeper than those of old planets
They have no orbital motion around their stars
They retain strong internal heat and are self-luminous in infrared wavelengths
Their atmospheres contain no clouds

text: What is angular differential imaging used to suppress?
choices: The planet's orbital eccentricity
The star's intrinsic infrared emission
Cosmic expansion in a radial-velocity spectrum
Quasi-static starlight speckles by exploiting field rotation

text: What does Gaia astrometry add to some exoplanet studies?
choices: Long-baseline position measurements can constrain a planet's orbit and true mass
It detects only atmospheres during secondary eclipse
It measures planets exclusively by microlensing
It eliminates the need for stellar distances

text: What is a transit injection–recovery test used to estimate?
choices: Whether a planet has a liquid ocean
How efficiently a survey would detect synthetic signals of different properties
The true abundance of oxygen in a star
The age of a telescope mirror

text: Why must occurrence-rate studies model a survey's window function?
choices: It measures the host star's magnetic field
It prevents all false positives automatically
Gaps and cadence determine which orbital periods could have been observed repeatedly
It converts radius into mass without assumptions

text: What is red noise in a transit light curve?
choices: Random photon noise with zero correlation
A spectrum containing only red wavelengths
Noise produced exclusively by red dwarf stars
Time-correlated systematic or astrophysical variation that can mimic transit structure

text: What is the stellar-density test for a transiting planet?
choices: The transit shape yields a density estimate that can be compared with independent stellar information
It determines the planet's atmospheric density from one spectral line
It counts the number of stars in the host galaxy
It measures only the star's metal content

text: Why can an unresolved eclipsing binary create a false planet radius?
choices: Binary eclipses cannot be periodic
Blended light dilutes its eclipse, while the wrong assumed host-star radius distorts the planetary interpretation
The binary always produces a larger radial-velocity amplitude than a planet
A companion star has no effect on photometry

text: What can transit timing variations reveal in a compact multi-planet system?
choices: The star's exact rotation period without stellar activity
The planets' surface colors directly
Planet masses and gravitational interactions through deviations from strict periodicity
Only the host star's distance

text: What is a transit duration variation (TDV) in exomoon searches?
choices: A change in a star's lifetime caused by a planet
A variation in atmospheric spectral resolution
A radial-velocity shift caused by stellar metallicity
A change in transit length that can arise from planet–moon orbital motion

text: Why can a planet's bulk density fail to identify its exact composition?
choices: Different mixtures of rock, metal, ice, and gas can share similar mass and radius
Density is independent of mass and radius
Only stars have measurable density
All planets with the same density have identical interiors

text: What is the mass function in a single-lined spectroscopic orbit?
choices: A direct map of the planet's surface mass
A combination of observable orbital parameters that constrains companion masses but retains inclination dependence
The number of planets in a transit catalog
A measure of the host star's atmospheric metallicity

text: What is spin–orbit misalignment?
choices: A planet rotating in the same direction as its star
A mismatch between a telescope's two mirrors
A difference between the star's spin axis and the planet's orbital angular-momentum direction
A disagreement between transit and eclipse depths

text: Why can the tidal disruption or Roche limit matter for ultra-short-period planets?
choices: It marks the distance where transits become impossible
It is the outer edge of every habitable zone
It determines only the star's spectral class
Inside it, stellar tides can overcome a planet's self-gravity and strip or disrupt the body

text: Why is the resonant chain in TRAPPIST-1 dynamically informative?
choices: The near-commensurate periods preserve evidence of migration and constrain planetary masses
It proves every planet has the same atmosphere
It makes their host star a blue giant
It prevents transit timing variations

text: What is Kozai–Lidov cycling in a hierarchical planetary system?
choices: A star alternates between two spectral classes
A distant inclined companion can exchange orbital inclination and eccentricity with an inner orbit
A planet's atmosphere cycles between oxygen and nitrogen
A transit repeats at twice the orbital frequency

text: What bias results from requiring several observed transits in a survey baseline?
choices: Short-period planets cannot transit
Large stars become invisible
Long-period planets are underrepresented because fewer of their transits occur during observations
Only planets with atmospheres are selected

text: What is the main degeneracy between atmospheric abundance and reference radius in transmission retrievals?
choices: Radius is measured only by radial velocity
Abundances never affect opacity
Reference radius is identical to the star's radius
Changing the assumed reference pressure or radius can trade off with inferred molecular abundance

text: Why are high-resolution cross-correlation spectra useful for exoplanet atmospheres?
choices: Many Doppler-shifted molecular lines can be combined to detect a faint moving planetary spectrum
They directly image the planet's continents
They remove the need for a host-star spectrum
They measure only the planet's transit depth

text: What is H-minus opacity especially important for in very hot atmospheres?
choices: It is the only source of molecular oxygen
Bound-free and free-free H− absorption can provide strong continuum opacity in ultra-hot planets
It causes all cool planets to become reflective
It measures a planet's orbital inclination

text: Why can the carbon-to-oxygen ratio be informative about formation?
choices: It uniquely determines a planet's surface gravity
It is independent of atmospheric chemistry
It can preserve clues about which gas and solid reservoirs contributed to a planet's envelope
It can be measured from transit timing alone

text: What is an energy-limited atmospheric escape estimate?
choices: A model in which a planet's energy is always conserved with no escape
A method for measuring orbital energy from a starspot
A calculation of reflected visible light only
A model balancing absorbed high-energy stellar power against the work needed to lift gas from the planet

text: Why can stellar activity bias a planet's transmission spectrum?
choices: Unocculted spots or faculae alter the star's apparent spectrum and transit baseline
Activity changes the planet's radius without changing observations
Flares occur only behind the planet
Stellar spectra contain no information during transit

text: Why can a habitable-zone estimate differ between researchers?
choices: The orbit's period changes every time a boundary is calculated
Clouds, atmospheric composition, stellar spectra, and climate-limit assumptions change the boundaries
The habitable zone is defined only by telescope aperture
All stars have identical luminosity

text: What does a planet's secondary-eclipse mapping or phase-curve offset indicate?
choices: It gives the planet's exact core radius
It identifies the star's birth cluster without a spectrum
It can constrain eastward or westward heat transport and the location of the hottest region
It proves the presence of a moon

text: What is the fundamental limitation of detecting an exoplanet by a single microlensing anomaly?
choices: Microlensing measures only planets with atmospheres
The anomaly always repeats after one orbital period
The method cannot detect planets beyond Earth
Different lens masses and geometries can produce similar light curves without additional constraints

text: What is the key selection effect in radial-velocity surveys favoring short-period planets?
choices: They complete more cycles during a finite observing campaign and produce easier-to-sample signals
They are always larger than long-period planets
Long-period planets have no gravitational effect
Short-period planets have no stellar jitter

text: What can asteroseismology contribute to exoplanet characterization?
choices: It directly detects radio emission from an exoplanet
Stellar oscillations can improve the host star's radius, density, and age estimates
It measures only the planet's atmospheric clouds
It replaces all transit observations

text: Why is an apparent oxygen feature not automatically a biosignature?
choices: Oxygen exists only on planets with life
Spectroscopy cannot detect oxygen
Abiotic photochemistry and geological processes can also produce oxygen or ozone
Oxygen is destroyed by every star

text: What combination would provide a stronger, though still model-dependent, life-related atmospheric case?
choices: A single broad brightness dip with no repetition
A planet's location outside every habitable zone
A high planetary mass alone
Multiple gases in chemical disequilibrium plus contextual evidence about the planet and star
